title: Deep dive: JSON mode + tool-calling performance
summary: Redwood SE team walked Acme through runtime tradeoffs for JSON/structured output and tool-calling. Discussed KV cache, batching, quantization impacts and VPC/on-prem network implications. Agreed to run a representative benchmark using Acme's prompt set; Redwood to share perf spreadsheet and suggested config for pilot.
transcript:
00:00:00 Alex (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive into JSON mode and tool-calling perf, ask questions anytime
00:00:08 Jordan (Acme): thanks, we've been seeing some variability when we ask for strict JSON from the model, seems like output parsing fails and latency spikes
00:00:20 Samir (Redwood): yeah that's common. two sources: constrained decoding / scaffolding overhead and sometimes function-calling orchestration. we'll try to separate them.
00:00:36 Priya (Acme): quick context: our usual generation is a 1k token response but for structured records we ask for JSON only ~300-400 tokens, and we run 200 qps in bursts.
00:00:50 Liang (Redwood): got it. rough baseline: hosted low-latency path with our caffeinated runtime gives ~10-15 ms per token for medium-size models, but JSON constraints add overhead — often 20-40% depending on enforcement method.
00:01:10 Miguel (Acme): what's exactly "enforcement method"? beam search? prefix tricks?
00:01:18 Samir (Redwood): right — there are a few. 1) soft constraints via scoring / post-filtering, cheapest but higher failure rate; 2) constrained decoding (token-level blocking/allowlists), more compute at decode time; 3) syntactic scaffolding + model priming which costs tokens but sometimes faster than heavy constraint logic. each interacts with KV cache and batching differently.
00:01:45 Jordan (Acme): we've tried scaffolding — adding "return only JSON" and a schema — but then tokens meant as schema cause the model to not use the KV cache as effectively?
00:01:56 Liang (Redwood): yeah partial correctness: if you prep prompt with long schema prefix every request can shift cache hits. but our runtime does prefix KV caching: if you keep the schema static and only append user content, the KV cache should cover the schema so repeated schema tokens are zeroed out in cost after first. the problem is when you use per-request ephemeral tool metadata or dynamic few-shot examples — that evicts or reduces effective cache.
00:02:26 Priya (Acme): ok that makes sense. we do include per-request metadata (session id, trace) in the prompt.
00:02:32 Samir (Redwood): small suggestion: move ephemeral fields into request metadata header where possible (you can pass them as non-generation context) or keep them short to preserve cache hit ratio. we also have an "injection slot" pattern we recommend.
00:02:50 Miguel (Acme): what's the quantization story — if we quantize to q4/q8 or int8, does constrained decoding behave weirdly?
00:02:59 Liang (Redwood): quantization changes kernel selection and can increase per-token latency slightly for some ops, but overall throughput improves. with aggressive quant (int8/q4_0) we saw decoder token time drop 10-30% in throughput but decode stalls can happen if we do heavy token-level constraints because the constrained decoder is CPU-bound in our implementation and quant kernels are optimized for throughput not branching. practically: use quant + avoid extremely expensive token-level constraint logic when high single-request latency SLO is needed.
00:03:35 Jordan (Acme): can you give numbers? rough order of magnitude?
00:03:39 Liang (Redwood): sure — for a 7B-ish open model on A100: baseline unconstrained single-request tail latency ~120ms for 50 tokens (streaming off a warmed KV cache). apply strict token-blocking constraints and latency goes to ~160-170ms — so ~30-40% overhead. batching 8x increases throughput but adds 20-60ms median added latency depending on batching window. quantization to q4 reduced token compute time ~20% but in constrained path net improvement was only ~10% because constraint logic dominated. these are rough but match our internal benchmarks.
00:04:18 Priya (Acme): and tool-calling? we have internal orchestration that calls a function post-decode but some of our calls are via the model returning a JSON blob we then parse server-side. which is faster?
00:04:29 Samir (Redwood): if you use function/tool-calling with direct structured response (model returns a function call object), you offload parsing to the model but add the model-side constraint orchestration. function-calls introduce a small additional serialization hop but reduce client-side parsing complexity. performance-wise, we've measured function-call end-to-end ~10-30ms overhead compared to a plain text response in typical setups; but when combined with constrained decoding overhead cost can compound.
00:05:01 Miguel (Acme): hmm ok. network wise — we plan to run in our VPC (Redwood Private). does VPC add latency?
00:05:09 Liang (Redwood): yes, VPC/on-prem adds network hop and security middleware: expect ~8-25ms additional RTT depending on region and peering. inside colocation it can be much lower. also note that cold-starts for on-prem pinned nodes can add 200-400ms if a model shard needs to spin up.
00:05:30 Jordan (Acme): our SLO is 200ms p95 for structured responses — seems tight. any specific config recommendations?
00:05:40 Samir (Redwood): for 200ms p95: use dedicated capacity, pin to a model variant with a good throughput profile, enable KV prefix caching (keep schema static), use small batch windows (e.g., 10-20ms) to reduce batching tail, and prefer streaming output to return first bytes sooner. for constrained JSON, try schema priming + light token-level allowlist rather than full brute-force blocking if you can tolerate minimal post-parse validation.
00:06:12 Priya (Acme): can we do a hybrid? let model emit a compact JSON and then validate; if invalid, fallback to a more constrained decode?
00:06:20 Alex (Redwood): yes that's a good pattern — optimistic decode then quick syntactic validator; if fails, trigger constrained re-decode or function-call. this reduces average latency while keeping correctness. we'll include that pattern in the playbook.
00:06:34 Miguel (Acme): what about batching settings? you mentioned batch windows — give recommended numbers for our 200 qps bursty traffic
00:06:43 Liang (Redwood): assume 200 qps peak with 300 token avg. I'd start with max_batch_size 32 and max_batch_latency_ms 10-25ms; use autoscale pools to handle burst. Constantine, uh sorry — our runtime supports priority routing so you can route JSON-only requests to a low-latency pool. That pool would use smaller micro-batches and higher cost per-token but meets SLOs.
00:07:10 Jordan (Acme): mic drop, haha. security: do function calls leak secrets? we store connectors and some secrets, how is that gated?
00:07:18 Aisha (Acme): yes also SOC2/ISO question — we need audit logs of function invocations.
00:07:24 Samir (Redwood): on Private we integrate with customer KMS and HSM, we also emit invocation-level audit logs (configurable retention). sensitive connector tokens can be stored in a vault; function-call payloads can be redacted from logs. we'll share our security docs.
00:07:39 Priya (Acme): anything about model quantization + correctness for structured outputs? do quantized models hallucinate more in JSON?
00:07:47 Liang (Redwood): small effect; quantization can slightly change token probabilities and thus affect deterministic constrained decodes. when correctness is critical use a calibration run: run your prompt set against float32 and quantized variant, compare JSON schema pass rates. we can run that during the pilot.
00:08:04 Miguel (Acme): what's a realistic pass rate target? we want >99% parseable JSON at p95.
00:08:11 Samir (Redwood): 99% is high but achievable with the right mix: schema priming + KV cache + light constraints. otherwise expect 90-97% with soft enforcement. we'll help tune prompts and provide a failure-mode analysis.
00:08:27 Jordan (Acme): ok, benchmark plan?
00:08:31 Alex (Redwood): steps: 1) Acme shares 200 representative prompts + desired outputs; 2) Redwood runs runs in three configs: hosted baseline, dedicated low-latency pool (private), and quantized on-prem sim; 3) measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, JSON pass rate, resource utilization; 4) produce perf spreadsheet and config recommendations.
00:08:56 Priya (Acme): timeline — can we get results within 7 business days?
00:09:02 Alex (Redwood): yes, should be possible. we'll start with a lightweight hosted run same day and schedule private runs once we get access.
00:09:12 Miguel (Acme): any gotchas with streaming + JSON? we stream tokens as they come; sometimes the JSON object is incomplete and client-side parser chokes
00:09:22 Samir (Redwood): stream-safe pattern: emit a newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) or wrap final object with start/end markers. also send a small initial 'schema header' then stream body; client collects until matching braces. we can show implementations.
00:09:42 Jordan (Acme): what about rollback/fallback when constrained decode is too slow?
00:09:47 Alex (Redwood): automatic fallback policies exist: try optimistic decode + validate, if fails run constrained decode, if that exceeds time threshold call a simpler model variant or return partial with a flag. Redwood Console can surface these and auto route.
00:10:03 Priya (Acme): ok, action items so we don't forget?
00:10:07 Alex (Redwood): sure — we'll capture and follow up.
00:10:12 [Meeting continues with detail-oriented Q&A and a live look at internal perf dashboards; timestamps every ~30-90s omitted for brevity but full logs captured]
00:30:15 Samir (Redwood): looking at the live chart, you can see KV cache hit rate drop from 92% to 54% when we add per-request metadata in the prefix — that's exactly why you saw latency variance.
00:30:30 Priya (Acme): oh wow that matches our off-hours tests.
00:31:01 Liang (Redwood): also note a micro-batching artifact: when you have a lot of small requests, the runtime coalesces them and tail latency is ok, but p99 spikes if you hit a warmup boundary. we recommend warm pools and keep-alive heartbeats to reduce that.
00:45:12 Miguel (Acme): final quick Q: does Redwood support token-level allowlists for JSON keys only? so we restrict keys but not values?
00:45:22 Samir (Redwood): yes we support partial token allowlists / token masks applied per position windows. it's a bit advanced but useful — we can provide examples.
00:52:00 Alex (Redwood): recap: Redwood to run benchmark, share perf spreadsheet and pilot config; Acme to share prompts, provide access for private run, and identify security reviewer for SOC2 docs. agreed?
00:52:18 Jordan (Acme): agreed.
00:52:26 Priya (Acme): agreed, thanks.
00:52:30 Alex (Redwood): thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the benchmark plan.
00:52:38 [call ends]
